title: Counting
idea: Give each thing one number word, in order. The last word says how many.
explain: Point at each thing once and say the numbers in order: one, two, three. Never skip a thing and never count one twice. The last number you say is how many there are, however you arranged them.
question: You touch each cup once: one, two, three, four, five. How many cups are there?

title: Zero
idea: Zero, written 0, is the count of nothing at all.
explain: Counting answers "how many?", and sometimes the answer is none. That count is zero. It comes just before one, so counting really starts from an empty table: 0, then 1, 2, 3 as things arrive.
question: A bowl holds 2 apples. Both are eaten. How many apples are in the bowl?

title: The number line
idea: The counting numbers in order along a line, one equal step apart, starting at 0.
explain: Put 0 at the left end of a line, then mark 1, 2, 3 and on to the right, every step the same length. A number's place on the line is how many steps it is from 0, so a number further right is bigger.
question: On a number line, how many steps is it from 0 to 6?

title: Adding
idea: Adding is stepping to the right on the number line: counting on.
explain: To work out 5 + 3, start at 5 on the number line and take 3 steps right: 6, 7, 8. Don't start again from 0; count on from where you are. Where you land is the total.
question: Start at 6 and step 3 to the right. What is 6 + 3?

title: Subtracting
idea: Subtracting is stepping to the left: it undoes adding.
explain: To work out 9 - 3, start at 9 and take 3 steps left: 8, 7, 6. It undoes the adding you just learned: 6 + 3 = 9, so 9 - 3 = 6. It also measures a gap: from 6 up to 9 is 3 steps.
question: You have 15 stickers and give away 6. How many are left?

title: Tens
idea: Ten ones bundled together make one ten.
explain: Stepping one at a time gets slow past 10, so count in bundles. Ten sticks tied together are one ten; adding or taking away a bundle is a jump of 10 steps at once. 23 sticks are 2 tens and 3 loose ones.
question: 47 sticks: how many bundles of ten, and how many loose?

title: Place value
idea: Where a digit stands says what it's worth: ones, tens, hundreds.
explain: Writing numbers in bundles: the right-hand digit counts ones, the next counts tens, the next hundreds (ten tens). In 347 the 3 is worth 300, the 4 is worth 40 and the 7 is worth 7. Each place is worth ten of the place on its right.
question: What is the 5 worth in 352?

title: Adding by place
idea: Add ones to ones and tens to tens; ten ones make a new ten.
explain: For 36 + 47, add each place on its own. Ones: 6 + 7 = 13, which is 1 ten and 3 ones. Tens: 3 + 4 = 7, and the new ten makes 8. So 83. Carrying is just rebundling ten ones into a ten.
question: What is 58 + 25?

title: Equal groups
idea: Multiplying is adding equal groups: 3 × 4 is three groups of 4.
explain: 3 bags of 4 apples is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, written 3 × 4 = 12. Adding the same number over and over is so common it gets its own sign. The order doesn't matter: 4 groups of 3 is also 12.
question: 5 boxes hold 6 eggs each. How many eggs?

title: Sharing equally
idea: Dividing shares into equal groups; it undoes multiplying.
explain: 12 ÷ 3 asks: share 12 among 3, how many each? Since 3 groups of 4 make 12, each gets 4. Dividing undoes multiplying the way subtracting undoes adding: 3 × 4 = 12, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
question: 20 sweets are shared equally by 4 children. How many each?

title: Remainders
idea: When a share doesn't come out even, what's left over is the remainder.
explain: Share 13 sweets among 4: each gets 3, which uses 12, and 1 is left over. We write 13 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 1. A remainder is always smaller than the number you share by; if it weren't, everyone could have one more.
question: 17 pencils shared by 5 people: how many each, and how many left?

title: Fractions
idea: A fraction is one or more equal parts of a whole.
explain: A leftover that can be cut can still be shared. Cut a pizza into 4 equal slices and each slice is one quarter, written 1/4. The parts must be equal: one of 4 unequal pieces is not a quarter.
question: A cake is cut into 8 equal slices. What fraction is one slice?

title: Top and bottom
idea: The bottom number says how many equal parts make the whole; the top, how many you have.
explain: In 3/8, the bottom (the denominator) says the whole is cut into 8 equal parts; the top (the numerator) says you have 3 of them. A bigger bottom number means smaller parts: eighths are smaller than quarters.
question: Which is bigger: one fifth or one tenth?

title: Fractions on the line
idea: Cut the step from 0 to 1 into equal parts: each mark is a fraction.
explain: Fractions live on the number line too. Cut the step from 0 to 1 into 5 equal parts: the bottom number says how many parts, and the top says how many you walk. 2/5 is two of those small steps from 0.
question: The step from 0 to 1 is cut into 4 equal parts. You walk 3. Where are you?

title: Whole ones
idea: When the top equals the bottom, the fraction is exactly 1.
explain: Walk all 4 quarter-steps and you reach 1: 4/4 = 1. Keep walking and you pass it: 5/4 is one whole and one quarter, written 1 1/4. A fraction whose top is bigger than its bottom is more than one whole.
question: Write 7/4 as a whole number and a fraction.

title: Same amount, new name
idea: Cut every part into equal smaller parts: the fraction's name changes, not its amount.
explain: Cut each half of a pizza into 2 and you have 4 quarters; one half is now 2 quarters. So 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6: multiply the top and the bottom by the same number, and you land on the same point of the line.

title: Simplest form
idea: Divide the top and bottom by the same number to get the simplest name.
explain: Going the other way: 6/8 has top and bottom both divisible by 2, so 6/8 = 3/4. When no number but 1 divides both, the fraction is in its simplest form. It's the same amount with the smallest numbers.
question: Write 6/9 in its simplest form.

title: Comparing fractions
idea: Give two fractions the same bottom number, then compare the tops.
explain: 3/5 beats 2/5: same-sized parts, and more of them. For 2/3 and 3/4, rename both in twelfths: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. Now the parts match, and 9/12 is bigger, so 3/4 is.
question: Which is bigger: 3/4 or 5/8?

title: Adding fractions
idea: With the same bottom number, add the tops; otherwise rename first.
explain: 1/5 + 2/5 = 3/5: same-sized parts, so count them. For 1/2 + 1/3 the parts differ, so rename both in sixths, as you did to compare them: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Never add the bottoms.

title: A fraction of an amount
idea: To find 3/4 of 12, divide by the bottom, then multiply by the top.
explain: 1/4 of 12 is 12 shared in 4: 3. Then 3/4 of 12 is three of those quarters added up: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9. So divide by the bottom number to find one part, then multiply by the top.
question: What is 2/5 of 20?

title: What fraction is it?
idea: A part of a group as a fraction: the part on top, the whole group below.
explain: Turned around: if 6 of 10 cars are blue, the blue ones are 6/10 of the cars, which simplifies to 3/5. Check it with what you just learned: 3/5 of 10 is 6.
question: 4 of 12 marbles are red. What fraction are red, in simplest form?

title: Ratio
idea: A ratio compares one part with another part, written 3 : 5.
explain: A fraction compares a part with the whole group; a ratio compares one part with another. A bag of 3 red and 5 blue marbles has red to blue in the ratio 3 : 5. Order matters: blue to red is 5 : 3.
question: A class has 12 girls and 13 boys. What is the ratio of boys to girls?

title: Ratio to fraction
idea: Add the parts of a ratio to find the whole: 3 : 5 makes red 3/8.
explain: If red to blue is 3 : 5, then for every 3 red there are 5 blue, 8 marbles in all. So red is 3/8 of the bag and blue 5/8. Add the ratio's parts to get the bottom number.
question: Boys to girls is 2 : 3. What fraction of the group are boys?

title: Equivalent ratios
idea: Multiply both parts of a ratio by the same number: the mix stays the same.
explain: Squash made 1 : 4 (squash to water) tastes the same as 2 : 8 or 3 : 12: the fraction of squash is 1/5 every time. It's the same rule as for equivalent fractions: do the same to both parts.

title: Simplest ratio
idea: Divide both parts by the same number to write a ratio simply.
explain: 12 : 8 shares a factor of 4 in both parts, so 12 : 8 = 3 : 2. As with fractions, a ratio is in its simplest form when no number but 1 divides both parts.
question: Write 10 : 15 in its simplest form.

title: Sharing in a ratio
idea: Add the ratio's parts, find one part's worth, then multiply.
explain: Share 20 sweets in the ratio 3 : 2. There are 3 + 2 = 5 parts, so one part is 20 ÷ 5 = 4 sweets. One person gets 3 × 4 = 12 and the other 2 × 4 = 8. Check: 12 + 8 = 20.
question: Share 30 in the ratio 2 : 3.

title: Unit rate
idea: How much for one: divide to get a rate per one.
explain: A ratio between two kinds of thing, like dollars to kilos, is a rate. Finding one part's worth gives the rate per one, the unit rate: 4 kg for $12 is 12 ÷ 4 = $3 per kg.
question: 6 pens cost $18. What does one pen cost?

title: Using a unit rate
idea: Multiply the unit rate by how many you want.
explain: Once you know the cost of one, any amount is a multiplication. At $3 per kg, 7 kg cost 7 × $3 = $21. That's two steps for any "if this, then that" question: divide to get one, multiply to get many.
question: 4 tickets cost $20. What do 7 tickets cost?

title: Speed
idea: Speed is a unit rate: the distance covered in one hour.
explain: A car that covers 150 km in 3 hours covers 150 ÷ 3 = 50 km in each hour: its speed is 50 km per hour, written 50 km/h. It's the unit rate again, with kilometres and hours as the two kinds of thing.
question: A train goes 240 km in 4 hours. What is its speed?

title: Distance from speed
idea: Distance = speed × time.
explain: Using the rate: at 50 km/h, each hour adds 50 km, so 3 hours cover 3 × 50 = 150 km. Run the other way it's the last step's division: time = distance ÷ speed.
question: A cyclist rides at 15 km/h for 4 hours. How far?

title: Proportional
idea: Two amounts are proportional when their rate never changes: double one, double the other.
explain: At a steady 50 km/h, 1 hour gives 50 km, 2 hours 100 km, 6 hours 300 km. Distance and time are proportional: whatever you do to one (double it, triple it, halve it), the same happens to the other.
question: 3 notebooks cost $6. At the same price, what do 9 cost?

title: The constant
idea: In a proportion, y = k × x, and k is the unit rate.
explain: Proportional amounts always keep the same multiplier between them. Cost = 3 × kilos, distance = 50 × hours. That fixed number k is the constant of proportionality, and it's the unit rate you already know how to find.
question: y is always 4 times x. If x is 7, what is y?

title: Is it proportional?
idea: Divide y by x for every pair: if it's always the same k, it's proportional.
explain: Pairs (2, 6), (5, 15), (8, 24) give 6 ÷ 2 = 3, 15 ÷ 5 = 3, 24 ÷ 8 = 3: the same k each time, so they're proportional. One pair that breaks the pattern, like (7, 20), and they aren't.
question: Are (2, 10), (3, 15) and (6, 32) proportional?

title: The graph of a proportion
idea: Plotted, a proportion is a straight line through (0, 0).
explain: Plot each pair, x across and y up. Because y = k × x, every step across goes the same k steps up, so the points sit on a straight line, and x = 0 gives y = 0. A line that misses (0, 0) is not a proportion.
question: Which point must a proportion's graph pass through?

title: Map scales
idea: A map scale is a constant of proportionality: real distance = k × map distance.
explain: On a map where 1 cm stands for 5 km, every distance on the ground is 5 × its length on the map. That's a proportion with k = 5 (km per cm): its graph would be the straight line you just met.
question: 1 cm on the map is 5 km. Two towns are 4 cm apart. How far is that?

title: Scale factor
idea: Enlarge a shape by multiplying every length by the same number.
explain: A map shrinks every length by one scale; an enlargement grows every length by one. A 3 cm by 5 cm photo enlarged by a scale factor of 2 becomes 6 cm by 10 cm. The shape stays the same because every length keeps its ratio.
question: A 4 by 6 rectangle is enlarged so its short side is 12. How long is its long side?

title: Percent
idea: Per cent means per hundred: 35% is 35 out of 100.
explain: Percent scales every whole to 100, so different amounts can be compared on one scale. 35% means 35/100. 100% is the whole, 50% is half of it, and 25% a quarter.
question: Write 50% as a fraction in simplest form.

title: Fraction to percent
idea: Rename a fraction out of 100 and the top is the percent.
explain: Scale the fraction so the bottom is 100, as with any equivalent fraction: 3/4 = 75/100, so 3/4 is 75%. For 2/5, multiply top and bottom by 20: 40/100, which is 40%.
question: Write 3/5 as a percent.

title: Percent of an amount
idea: Find 1% or 10% first, then multiply.
explain: A percent of an amount is a fraction of it. 10% of 70 is 70 ÷ 10 = 7, so 30% of 70 is 3 × 7 = 21. Or turn the percent into a fraction first: 25% of 80 is 1/4 of 80, which is 20.
question: What is 30% of 50?

title: Percent change
idea: Work out the percent of the original amount, then add it or take it away.
explain: A $40 shirt at 25% off: 25% of $40 is $10, so it costs $40 - $10 = $30. A price rising by 10% from $40: add 10% of $40, which is $4, to get $44. The percent is always of the amount you started from.
question: A $60 game is 20% off. What does it cost?
